# Content Design Vision for Terminology

**Owner:** Central Content Design ([Kieran Forde](mailto:kiforde@hubspot.com))   
**Audience:** UX Directors, Platform & Systems leaders, Trellis, Central CD

Related:  
[Terminology: Technical Reference](https://docs.google.com/document/u/0/d/1ngLlz6Iv8WIzjNdBrQvRT6NV_s4XKTDbjrje3ItEWF4/edit)  
[Technical Requirements: Content Design Tooling](https://docs.google.com/document/u/0/d/1vBvmB2rb-GvBsz4yFfhlQS2kqdbB7QzT7JSN0V2dnXg/edit)  
[\[2026\] Central Content Design strategy](https://docs.google.com/document/u/0/d/1ZXJCUemsubfUssPyzTPg1C2r6uY9Y4_HoO24jbD1M-Y/edit)

# 1\. Summary

Right now, terminology is a major UX quality issue that makes HubSpot harder to use. This document looks at the tools we are building to identify terminology problems, and how we will explore ways to fix them at scale.

## Goals for this vision

* Capture the terminology problems we’re solving  
* Show what “good” looks like for the next 6–12 months  
* Set a roadmap for Q1 and Q2  
* Align with Central Content Design 2026 vision and strategy, particularly our focus on [content metrics](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1VFb1wrAlofdBZ2rGHBWEk9euAXQlJ3du9OOmaKMnnBc/edit?tab=t.yvegpr8kcf3b)

## Why This Matters

### Terms are a huge part of building consistent, crafted product experiences

Terms matter, because they’re the most atomic units of content in our designs. Terms describe HubSpot-specific concepts in our product system and brand, ensuring that we talk about concepts in the right way. This makes our product simpler, clearer, and far more consistent. 

Terms are part of our design system and, like UI components, we want them to be simple, standard, and used consistently. The difference is, if our UI components are inconsistent, we see it immediately. If our terms are inconsistent, users feel it, support hears it, but we don’t have ways to identify or quantify it.

When terms drift, we get:

* Confusing cross‑hub journeys; take [“leads” for example](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/12GXo9o0l-ULZk3bPLBB6GQ8EmzZHyWI_3XQP6hWjJzA/edit?slide=id.g3409d4d6448_0_574#slide=id.g3409d4d6448_0_574) \- in Marketing Hub a lead is a potential customer, yet in Sales Hub it’s a sales attempt, linked to revenue. Customers need to understand that one term can mean two things.  
* Inaccurate Breeze responses; when terms have multiple meanings, Breeze can say things that are [technically correct, but illogical](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/12GXo9o0l-ULZk3bPLBB6GQ8EmzZHyWI_3XQP6hWjJzA/edit?slide=id.g34114d945b6_0_410#slide=id.g34114d945b6_0_410)  
* [Extra support and CSM volume](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/12GXo9o0l-ULZk3bPLBB6GQ8EmzZHyWI_3XQP6hWjJzA/edit?slide=id.g3416cbb5807_1_10056#slide=id.g3416cbb5807_1_10056) in high‑value areas

# 2\. Problem

## Customer and product signals

* Terminology debt is a big UX problem  
  * Around 86% of Writer suggestions to UXers are terminology issues and Writer surfaces \~1.3M term‑based issues to UXers every week  
  * We know there are big gaps in our terminology documentation, so even these significant stats don’t capture all the situations where terms issues exist, or are being introduced to the product.  
* Customers are telling us the same story  
  * Analysis of 12 months of CSAT and pNPS survey data identified [37 confirmed terminology complaints](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bOXFC0d64Sw11DOH11WOHLyD2WAvutMJhPCIQjdpNV8/edit) spanning five distinct themes: explicit terminology confusion, unclear wording, inconsistent naming conventions, frustrating renames, and misleading labels.   
  * The average CSAT score for these complaints is 2.6 out of 5, and complaints appear across multiple product areas and on a frequent, consistent basis  
  * Customers describe the problem directly. One wrote that HubSpot's *"terminology and labels are often in conflict between areas."* Another said *"everything is mislabelled — it feels like this was not built with humans in mind."*   
  * Support calls surface cases where a single name caused measurable harm: the "Lists" to "Segments" rename broke day-to-day workflows for multiple customers, and a button labelled "Complete Purchase" caused a customer to delay a renewal out of fear of being charged immediately.  
  * The root causes that drove Code Orange — poor usability and high product complexity — are significantly affected by inconsistent terminology. This was [highlighted in the Code Orange UX all-team](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1-1DRv3zyF_uHiP8WDwD7nqBWQw8-xNM7pXe5v2h3gU0/edit?slide=id.g3a00dbe6690_0_2501#slide=id.g3a00dbe6690_0_2501).

For the full evidence base — including methodology, source data, and detailed analysis — see [Voice of the Customer](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bOXFC0d64Sw11DOH11WOHLyD2WAvutMJhPCIQjdpNV8/edit). 

## Opportunities and challenges

* Since content design was re-organized into a central structure, very few (less than 20\) new terms have been submitted to Writer by non-content designers, even as teams introduce and change core terms.  
* We have guidance and Writer, but:  
  * Terminology documentation is patchy and [uneven across product lines](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/16d82vp2dcka93TBVVReugk1_NB4vHSADB2NXo95BoG8/edit?slide=id.g32b1c11aaf6_0_2#slide=id.g32b1c11aaf6_0_2)  
  * Very few people are actively defining new terms or snippets  
  * Guidance on its own hasn’t created enough momentum to fix conflicts at scale  
* We developed [terminology workshops](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/16d82vp2dcka93TBVVReugk1_NB4vHSADB2NXo95BoG8/edit?slide=id.g329985a2d1e_2_21#slide=id.g329985a2d1e_2_21) to identify new terms   
  * The workshops are effective (three pilot sessions surfaced **\~27 terms** in an hour per team)  
  * Without a Content Designer driving, teams are not running workshops; building a governance structure that would see all teams running regular workshops was seen as a heavy lift  
  * We had feedback from UX Leadership to that we needed to be clearer what winning/completion would look like  
* We developed the [terminology checker](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1q3RBh-Pc4Q8LPeqV0e-N6iJn59UaH2hSgeDPMGczAhw/edit?slide=id.g3aff5daf65c_0_3122#slide=id.g3aff5daf65c_0_3122) app, which finds term issues and potential new terms directly from product strings.  
  * It captures 100% of terminology errors in the product, and about 85% of potential new terms that need to be documented (compared to a manual audit), reducing months of work to seconds.  
* Using the terminology checker app to pilot terminology audits during Code Orange gave us a baseline:  
  * Auditing Automation, Data Hub, and Reporting code repositories, we found 1,673 incorrect uses of terms and 3,638 potential new terms to document.  
  * Even with considerable time spent identifying, contacting, and following up with the relevant teams, response to these issues has been limited  
  * We need mechanisms to speed up routing issues to teams, and potentially to fix clear-cut error directly

# 3\. Vision

## Vision for 2026

By the end of 2026, terminology will be supported by a repeating Find/Fix/Define/Report loop that continuously reduces terminology debt across the product, with clear ownership and dashboards that teams and leadership trust.

To support this, we will develop processes and systems for HubSpot terminology that:

* Regularly scans the product codebase to **find** terminology issues  
* Makes it safe and straightforward to **fix** them in code or through automated notifications with a clear feedback loop  
* Makes it easy to **define** new terms, automatically or using simple guidance that makes it quick to contribute quality terminology documentation  
* **Reports** on the state of terminology in the product, so that we can measure progress and quality over time

As a general principle, we will prioritise automated fixes that are owned by CD wherever possible.

## Terminology loop

* **Find**  
  * Run Terminology Checker on product repos to find:  
    * Incorrect uses of existing terms  
    * Deprecated or forbidden terms  
    * Terms that “look like” they should be in Writer but aren’t yet  
  * Mine customer feedback sources (support, CSAT, PM Sidekick, Reforge) for language and comprehension issues.  
* **Fix**  
  * Turn audits and feedback into clear sets of changes, which could include:  
    * Content‑only PRs where safe  
    * Well‑scoped tickets where teams need to implement the fix  
    * Automated Slack notifications to ask relevant people for approval or action  
* **Define**  
  * Use AI with access to sufficient HubSpot context to generate simple definitions   
  * Use **self‑serve workshops** so product lines decide on more complex terms and definitions together.  
  * Send agreed terms to Central CD for review and add them to our central database as the canonical course.  
* **Report**  
  * Create a simple, shared view of terminology issues and documentation for each product area (terms in Writer, open issues, fixes shipped).  
  * Share short, visual updates with teams and UX leadership every quarter so progress is visible.  
  * Use these reports to decide where to focus next, and when pilots are ready to scale.

# 4\. Key risks and design questions

For more details exploration of technical considerations, go to [Terminology Tooling: Technical Reference](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ngLlz6Iv8WIzjNdBrQvRT6NV_s4XKTDbjrje3ItEWF4/edit?usp=sharing)

## Technical

* How can we build the app in a way that meets HubSpot’s infrastructure requirements, and host it using safe, compliant systems that relevant HubSpotters can access?  
* How will we store app data in a scalable format that allows regular “whole-product” scans that enable us to build dashboards that track progress over time?  
* How can we connect the app to relevant external systems: Writer, SideKick, Slack, GitHub, Monarch, so that repeating actions can be automated?  
* What level of automation is possible and appropriate? Currently, manual steps include:   
  * Scanning product repositories for strings  
  * Mapping strings to product areas  
  * Uploading strings to the app  
  * Exporting reports  
  * Identifying relevant teams/individuals/Slack channels to contact  
  * Sending reports and actions, chasing updates

## Process

What is required to make a case to relevant HubSpot engineering teams to rebuild the app on internal systems with sufficient features to support our vision?

Which metrics reflect our terminology goals so that we can track progress over time?

How does the process of Find/Fix/Define map against real world team processes?

* What criteria will we use to decide whether teams should be responsible, accountable, consulted, or informed about term changes and definitions?  
  * How will we delegate actions to teams and track progress?

Can we secure leadership backing and sponsorship to support terminology governance and hold teams accountable for taking action to improve terminology issues?

# 5\. What “Good” Looks Like

## Project progress

In Q1, we will explore the technical and process requirements for the project. This will enable us to clearly define how we will achieve the vision; specifically, which parts of the process are manual or automated, and which are owned by CD or delegated.

![][image1]

As part of this, we will build a proof of concept that pilots the end-to-end process with a specific product area, such as Platform and Systems teams. 

## UX/Terminology progress

### Terminology errors in the live product are decreasing

The terminology checker identifies fewer issues in consecutive monthly scans, showing that fixes are outpacing new debt. This is the most direct measure of whether the Find/Fix loop is having an effect.

### New terms are being documented at a steady rate. 

The number of terms defined and added to Writer increases over consecutive months, closing the documentation gaps that make future scans incomplete. Without this, the checker can only catch known issues, whilst the unknown ones keep shipping.

### Teams are contributing to terminology governance without CD driving every session.

Product teams are running workshops on a regular cadence, and the proportion of flagged terms categorised as "needs review" is falling — meaning teams are resolving ambiguity closer to the source.

### Customer-reported terminology confusion is declining. 

Support interactions where customers explicitly cite confusing wording, labels, or terminology show a measurable reduction. This is the hardest metric to move, because it depends on fixes reaching production and customers noticing the difference — but it's the one that matters most.

### People across the org can find the right term without guessing. 

PDs, PMs, and engineers can answer "What's the right term here?" by following a clear, documented process — not by starting a Slack thread or making their best guess. This is qualitative, but observable: fewer ad-hoc terminology questions in Slack channels, and more references to the terminology database in design reviews and PRs.

# 6\. Dependencies

| Dependency | Mitigation |
| :---- | :---- |
| Finding an engineering team to support rebuilding the app on internal infrastructure | Bridge the gap with third-party tools, like Lovable and Supabase (or new Hubbable features) whilst building the internal case |
| Technical solutions that enable the end-to-end process to run on a regular cadence, with appropriate, scalable data storage | Manual runs, re-runs, and processes to track change over time, which will build evidence for better tooling |
| Backing/approval to build tooling that ships code changes and/or PRs automatically | Fallback to Slack automations to route requests to people/teams, or manually messaging and chasing teams for updates. This is not a sustainable long-term approach, but could help build evidence for investment. |
| Commitment from product teams to respond to recommendations and requests from content design and our team’s systems/tools | No mitigation for this \- terminology cannot improve without automation and/or teams’ commitment to make changes |

# Roadmap

# Roadmap

This roadmap is subject to progress of the related workstream to build CD tooling on HubSpot infrastructure: [Technical Requirements: Content Design Tooling](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1vBvmB2rb-GvBsz4yFfhlQS2kqdbB7QzT7JSN0V2dnXg/edit?tab=t.0)

# High-level milestones

## By the end of January

* The key technical and process questions (hosting, data storage, Sidekick-generated PRs/CD direct deployment, metrics, RACI) are answered, or have clear owners who can answer them, with small technical spikes to validate during Q1.  
* A narrow proof-of-concept scope is chosen: one product area and one class of issues that we can try to automate end-to-end.

## By the end of February

* Technical spikes have run for:  
  * **Data \+ scans** – options for storing results and running repeat scans at scale (even if rough/temporary).  
  * **Sidekick/PRs** – whether we can reliably turn app output into draft PRs for simple fixes.  
  * **Integrations** – what it would take to connect to Writer, Slack, and GitHub for automated follow-up.  
* For each step in the Find/Fix/Define loop, there's a first pass at "manual vs automatable," with risks and unknowns called out.

## By the end of March

* A short **Technical & Process Design** doc answers the key questions: recommended hosting direction (bridge vs long-term), data storage pattern, and key integration points; which steps will be automated vs human-driven.  
* A draft Terminology OS / RACI shows: how the Find/Fix/Define loop maps to real team workflows; who is responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed about different categories of issue; how relevant people will be identified and notified about changes.  
* One small end-to-end pilot has run under this OS, automating steps where possible and substituting with manual effort where not. Learnings will be folded back into the design.

## By the end of Q2

* One or two high-value steps are partially automated for pilots (e.g. repeat scans \+ centralised storage, or simpler report generation), based on the Q1 design decisions.  
* A basic dashboard is live for the pilot area(s) with real terminology metrics wired in (issues found, fixes shipped, early customer/support signals).  
* A clear "internal tool candidate" proposal exists for engineering: app architecture and technical approach, what features are essential, and what value we've proven.

## By the end of Q3

* Each pilot product line has completed at least one full Find/Fix/Define/Report cycle on the improved system, with measurable improvements vs baseline.  
* Decisions made on the long-term infrastructure, with partner buy-in.  
* The Terminology OS, metrics, and RACI are updated from pilot learning, with next steps for scaling.

# Phase 1 – Prove the loop: outcomes and decisions

**Validated the all-surfaces pipeline with Platform Engineering.** Met with Owen to confirm how the app connects to different surfaces and produces a unified dataset. This shaped the data pipeline design and confirmed we could scan across surfaces rather than repo-by-repo.

**Secured Claude Code access for local scripting and automation.** Requested through Jonathon Colman. This unblocked local automation work, including all-surfaces scanning and analysis scripts.

**Positioned the terminology checker as a use case for the AI acceleration P0 program.** Posted in \#devex-ai-p0-accelerate-product-teams-using-ai with a summary of the problem, the app's impact so far, and what's needed next. Tagged key stakeholders (bcrawford, zklapow, hemerson, nuge) to establish visibility with the program.

**Ran a manual Sidekick PR experiment to validate the fix mechanism.** Worked with Matt Roe to understand available resources. Selected a small, clear-cut change type (e.g. "HubSpot AI" → "Breeze"), exported flagged strings, and used Sidekick to draft PRs. Outcome: confirmed that app output → Sidekick → PR → merge is viable and safe, with manageable review effort.

**Published a canonical strategy document covering the full approach.** Updated the Terminology OS / Q1 design doc with a Now / Next / Later framework:

* **Now (Q1):** Manual audits, Sidekick PR experiment, Supabase/Lovable proof of concept.  
* **Next:** Slack bot \+ deeper metrics integration.  
* **Later:** Internal rebuild on HubSpot infrastructure (Hubbable/BLT, Monarch, Service Maturity).

# Phase 2 – Build the system: outcomes and next steps

**Defined a central data schema to support repeatable scans and dashboards.** Designed the structure to capture string context (ID, text, repo, file path, product area/service), classification (issue type, suggested fix), lifecycle (status, detection and scan dates), and ownership (team from CodeOwners, PM candidate from CXM matching).

**Stood up Supabase and mirrored the schema.** Created a Supabase project and table matching the schema. Ran a first test pushing data from an existing scan, confirming that non-PII scan results can be stored centrally and queried.

**Built a minimal Lovable dashboard on top of Supabase.** Delivered a first shared UI for exploring terminology issues, with filtering by product area or team, toggling between issue tiers, and basic metrics (open vs fixed issues by team/product area).

**Next: Plug terminology data into Kelly's Q1 metrics pilot.** Agree with Kelly how to compute a compliance score per product area from the Supabase table, and decide how she'll consume it (CSV export, dashboard embed, or integration into Looker/Hex). This makes "style & terminology compliance" a real metric in the content quality work.

**Next: Explore ownership routing via CodeOwners \+ CXM PM matching.** Use CodeOwners to auto-populate owner\_team for rows in the database. Set up time with Hannah Hoar to understand and, if possible, reuse the CXM PM-matching system to populate a pm\_candidate field, even as a batch process initially. Goal: fewer manual guesses when mapping strings to teams and PMs.

**Next: Clarify Slack bot/agent constraints.** Talk to Slack admins about what's allowed for a minimal first bot: periodic messages to the DRI with a link to the dashboard and simple approve/decline actions. Capture constraints and recommended patterns for future integration work.

# Phase 3 – Lock in long-term ownership and platform backing

**Next: Explore Monarch / Service Maturity integration.** Define what a terminology quality metric would look like per service, and identify one pilot service where scan output could feed a soft maturity score and/or a tightly scoped Monarch campaign for clear-cut issues.

**Next: Refine a RACI for Find → Fix → Define → Report.** Create a flow diagram showing actions and systems involved for different term types (e.g. clear-cut errors are automatically fixed, new terms are sent for review via Slack). Mark which parts of the loop are CD-owned (scans, Supabase, Sidekick PRs) and which are team-owned (approvals, complex term/docs work). Tie this to data fields and workflows so it's concrete, not abstract.

**Next: Prepare an internal rebuild pitch for BLT and Ben.** Package what's been proven (detection accuracy, manual pilot outcomes, Sidekick PR results, metrics integration with Kelly) alongside what the internal tool needs (hosting/auth on HubSpot infrastructure, integrations with Sidekick, Monarch, and Service Maturity, a minimal but robust UI for viewing, triaging, and tracking issues). Frame this as a fit for the P0 AI-acceleration program: org-wide leverage, reusable pattern for other quality checks.

**Next: Scale from a single pilot area into campaigns.** Once the loop works for one area, design a branding cleanup campaign (e.g. all "HubSpot AI" → "Breeze" fixes across hubs). Run the campaign end-to-end: scan, Sidekick PRs, tracking in Supabase, and a short before/after report.

# Voice of the Customer

# Voice of the customer

Multiple research sources show us that terminology \- the words, labels, and names used in the HubSpot product interface \- is a persistent, structural UX problem. 

The evidence comes from: 

* CSAT and pNPS survey analysis  
* Support call transcripts  
* Internal UX research  
* Synthesis of evidence gathered for [\[2026\] Central Content Design strategy](https://docs.google.com/document/u/0/d/1ZXJCUemsubfUssPyzTPg1C2r6uY9Y4_HoO24jbD1M-Y/edit), [Terminology: 2026 Content Design Vision](https://docs.google.com/document/u/0/d/1JCxwCp2xIHNivpBJLZeu14EvQ7vfx3USIjNWYVn7HjU/edit), and other recent content design resources

Each source was gathered and assessed independently. Together, they describe the same problem from different angles.

Detailed breakdown of research by source: [Terminology: voice of the customer research](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bOXFC0d64Sw11DOH11WOHLyD2WAvutMJhPCIQjdpNV8/edit?tab=t.h26yv9srndqt)

# What customers say in surveys

Over a 12-month period, we identified **37 confirmed terminology complaints** in CSAT and pNPS survey response, drawn from a keyword-filtered export of 108 responses and manually reviewed to exclude false positives. 

![][image2]

All five themes \- terminology confusion, inconsistent naming conventions, unclear wording, frustrating renames, and misleading labels \- appear across multiple months and product areas, with no month recording zero complaints. The average CSAT score for these complaints is **2.6 out of 5**, and more than a third scored 1 or 2\.

![][image3]

Customers describe the problem in strikingly direct terms. One wrote that HubSpot's *"[terminology and labels are often in conflict between areas.](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1f04qt8UXhvR4lPQVAfIRJNxXzPvu3RPvoo0DEaWyNPs/edit?gid=627039005#gid=627039005&range=F28)"* Another said *"[wording varies heavily](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1f04qt8UXhvR4lPQVAfIRJNxXzPvu3RPvoo0DEaWyNPs/edit?gid=627039005#gid=627039005&range=F19)."* A third said [*"everything is mislabelled — it feels like this was not built with humans in mind.*](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1f04qt8UXhvR4lPQVAfIRJNxXzPvu3RPvoo0DEaWyNPs/edit?gid=627039005#gid=627039005&range=F50)*"*

The even spread across five themes matters. This is not one team's naming problem or one badly chosen label. It is a product-wide pattern affecting naming, labelling, wording, and how we communicate change.

# What happens when terminology goes wrong

Support call analysis surfaces cases where a name — not a missing feature or a broken workflow — was the direct cause of a customer problem.

When "Lists" was renamed to "Segments," multiple customers called support because they could no longer find their existing lists. One spent a full week confused. One pNPS detractor wrote: *"Renaming of lists to segments had no upside, only downside. I spent a week searching and being confused in my daily work, for no gain."*

In another case, a button labelled "Complete Purchase" caused a customer to delay a renewal out of fear of being charged immediately. Inconsistent field names — "Phone Number" in one place, "Tell" in another — forced a team into manual workarounds. Two near-identical property names — "Country/Region" and "Country/Region Code" — caused data entry errors that required manual cleanup.

These are cases where the name of something caused a customer to do the wrong thing, avoid doing the right thing, or call support for help with something they should have been able to do on their own. Support ticket data shows approximately **270 terminology-related tickets per month** over six months, with no downward trend.

![][image4]

# What research tells us

Internal UX research consistently identifies terminology as a barrier to adoption and confidence. In a Breeze AI Agent Builder study, **35% of users reported feeling "not very confident"** about setting up an agent on their own, and the research directly attributes that low confidence to confusing terms like "Trigger" and "Knowledge." A separate agents content study concluded that *"terminology is the biggest determinant of user confidence."*

Synthesis of internal research and discussion surfaces cross-cutting patterns that go beyond individual terms. The same concept often has multiple names across the product: "Files," "Documents," and "Attachments" all refer to things customers think of as the same object, but each works differently in different contexts. One customer wrote: *"Very difficult to tell the difference between when I need a file vs. a document."* Similarly, "Landing pages" and "Website pages" create an artificial split that confuses customers who see the same function: *"I don't understand why new pages I create are sometimes created as landing pages vs. web pages."*

Scope words like "global," "default," and "corporate vs personal" fail to explain what they affect, leading to uncertainty and fear of editing. Implementation jargon — "modules," "wrappers," "sections" — leaks into the customer-facing UI, creating friction for people performing basic tasks. And object names hide functional requirements that customers only discover when something goes wrong: *"Isn't clear that CTAs need to be HubSpot CTAs."*

# What this evidence adds up to

Four independent evidence sources — survey data, support interactions, UX research, and internal synthesis — all converge on the same conclusion. Terminology is a measurable, persistent, product-wide UX problem that affects customer confidence, increases support load, and does not improve on its own.

The full evidence, methodology, and source data for each analysis is documented in the tabs that follow.
